The test image shows tomato plants on black plastic mulch with what appears to be 2-3 plants in the center that have completely collapsed/wilted to the ground, while surrounding plants remain upright and healthy. This pattern of sudden, localized collapse is characteristic of a soilborne wilt disease affecting the stem at the soil level.

Key observations:
- Whole plant collapse (not just leaf symptoms)
- Localized to adjacent plants in the row
- Plants appear to have fallen/wilted at the base
- No visible leaf spots or foliar disease patterns
- Black plastic mulch growing environment

This pattern is most consistent with **Southern Blight** (Sclerotium rolfsii) which causes stem girdling at the soil line leading to complete plant collapse. Let me view one reference image to confirm.

- Setting: Field-grown tomatoes on black plastic mulch

- Surrounding plants: Healthy and upright
- Pattern: Highly localized, patch-like distribution

**Reasoning:**
- Complete plant collapse (not just leaf wilting) points to a soilborne pathogen attacking the stem
- The localized patch pattern is characteristic of Sclerotium rolfsii (Southern Blight)
- Southern Blight is extremely common on plastic mulch-grown tomatoes — the mulch creates warm, moist conditions near the stem base
- Bacterial wilt diseases can cause similar collapse but tend to affect more plants simultaneously and progression is slightly different
- The fact that plants have literally toppled/fallen sideways is more consistent with stem girdling at the crown (Southern Blight) than vascular wilt alone
- Verticillium/Fusarium wilts would show slower, more gradual yellowing/wilting without this sudden collapse
